fixes.explanation: Micah says it plainly: “At morning’s light they accomplish it because the power is in their hands.” The plan made on the bed gets carried out when the light comes. That's what Micah's woe is aimed at, friend.
Micah 2:2 says, "They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses." Coveting and seizing show up in the same line, friend. Verse 1 already told us the power is in their hands.
Planting would be honest work, and I'd happily help! But Micah 2:2 says they "…covet fields and seize them…" and that they "…deprive a man of his home…" Planting isn't what the verse says they do.
Guarding a field is a fine job, friend. But Micah 2:2 says they "…covet fields and seize them…" and "…take away houses." Guarding isn't the word the verse uses.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "Then you will not walk so proudly, for it will be a time of calamity." Just before that, He speaks of "…a disaster from which you cannot free your necks." That's the LORD's word on how they will walk.
Careful, friend, because the card is quoting Micah 2:3. The LORD says, "Then you will not walk so proudly, for it will be a time of calamity." So He does say they will not walk so proudly.

That's what the lament says: "He has changed the portion of my people. How He has removed it from me!" The speakers say the portion has been removed from them. It goes on, "He has allotted our fields to traitors."
Thorns would be a sad end for a field, but Micah doesn't mention them here. The lament says, "How He has removed it from me!" The verse says the portion is removed, and that's what we stick with.

I can see why you'd think so, but Micah 2:5 says the opposite. It reads, "Therefore, you will have no one in the assembly of the LORD to divide the land by lot." So nobody in the assembly is there to do the dividing for them.
That's what they say, friend: "Do not preach these things; disgrace will not overtake us." They're sure disgrace won't overtake them. I bet that's a lot of confidence to pack into one sentence.

I get why the power talk might stick in your head after the last verses. But the LORD asks, "Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly?" The good is for the one who walks uprightly. This verse doesn't mention power at all.
Yes, friend. The LORD asks, "Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly?" The one the verse names is the person who walks uprightly. Power isn't mentioned there.

A widow isn't named in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "But of late My people have risen up like an enemy…" The same verse goes on to what they do: "You strip off the splendid robe from unsuspecting passersby…"

Swords are a fair guess because the verse mentions "…men returning from battle." But the verse says, "You strip off the splendid robe from unsuspecting passersby like men returning from battle." What gets stripped off is "…the splendid robe…"

Micah says it with a bit of a sting: "he would be just the preacher for this people!" This is about a man of wind who falsely says he will preach of wine and strong drink. I think that's the sharpest line in the chapter, friend.

Running him out of town isn't what the verse says, friend. Micah says a man of wind who falsely offers to preach of "…wine and strong drink…" "…would be just the preacher for this people!" Nothing in the verse mentions anyone running him off.

Testing him would be careful, but the text doesn't show that. It says a man of wind who falsely offers to preach of "…wine and strong drink…" "…would be just the preacher for this people!" No test is mentioned.
Camels aren't in this picture, friend. The LORD says, "I will bring them together like sheep in a pen, like a flock in the midst of its pasture…" It's sheep, and the remnant is what He's gathering.
Micah isn't the one leading here, friend. The verse says, "Their King will pass through before them, the LORD as their leader." The LORD is the one in front.
